explanation: Ammonites were cephalopods that swam in coiled, chambered shells. They filled the seas for a vast stretch of time and died out with the non-bird dinosaurs.

claims.text: The closest living relatives of ammonites are coleoid cephalopods such as squid and octopuses.
Ammonites were not more closely related to snails, slugs, crabs, lobsters, clams or oysters than to squid and octopuses.
Ammonites were cephalopods with coiled, chambered shells.
Ammonites died out at the end of the Cretaceous, along with the non-bird dinosaurs.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: four listed; high: c1 (superlative); standard: c2, c3 and c4. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology (it holds countries, languages, currencies, cities, elements, Nobel Prizes, Olympic Games, World Cups, art collections and Natural Earth), so none applies, and the high-risk claims need web evidence from checker A; one search on the closest living relatives of ammonites should cover c1 and c3. rivalTest: Argued for 'Snails and slugs', the obvious pick for a coiled shell and the reason counterintuitive is set. The nautilus was kept out of the options: it looks most like an ammonite, but most studies place ammonites closer to squid and octopuses, and offering both would invite a dispute. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: ammonite fossils are sold and found worldwide. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 26 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a multiple-choice item. doubts: c1 depends on phylogenies that put ammonoids with the coleoids rather than the nautiloids; that is the mainstream view, and the key avoids the nautilus so the item survives either way.

evidence.restatement: Ammonites were cephalopods closer to the living coleoids (squid, octopuses and cuttlefish) than to the nautilus.

evidence.restatement: As cephalopods, ammonites were closer to squid and octopuses than to snails, slugs, clams, oysters, crabs or lobsters.
Ammonites were cephalopods with coiled shells divided into chambers.
Ammonites died out in the end-Cretaceous extinction, along with the non-bird dinosaurs.
Ammonites are generally placed closer to the coleoid cephalopods (squid, octopuses, cuttlefish) than to the shelled nautiluses.

claimResults.note: Mainstream view. A minority of analyses disagree, but nautilus is not an option, so the key stands.

evidence.restatement: Ammonites are cephalopods, so they are closer to squid and octopuses than to snails, slugs, clams, oysters, crabs or lobsters.
Ammonites were cephalopods with coiled, chambered shells.
Ammonites died out at the end of the Cretaceous, with the non-bird dinosaurs.
